Hatfield.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of central Hertfordshire
s1loc: Hatfield runs a strong visitor economy built around Hatfield House, the great Jacobean mansion completed in 1611 by Robert Cecil and set in 42 acres of formal gardens, with the surviving Old Palace where Elizabeth the First spent much of her childhood standing alongside it. The estate's deer park, the woodland and the marble hall draw visitors year-round, anchoring the town as a marquee day-out destination on the northern edge of Greater London.

The leisure and activity layer reaches across the surrounding parkland and waterways. Stanborough Park and its lakes nearby offer sailing, kayaking and pedalo hire, while the Hatfield watermill on the River Lea grinds flour by techniques over a thousand years old, and the trails of the Hatfield House parkland and the Mill Green common give families and activity operators a busy outdoor offer through the warmer season across the wider district.

Heritage and culture run deep here, from the historic Old Hatfield quarter climbing Fore Street to St Etheldreda's Church beside the great house. The de Havilland aviation story, with the Comet and Mosquito built at the old Hatfield Aerodrome, gives the town a distinctive industrial identity, while Mill Green Museum in the restored mill and the events staged across the Hatfield House grounds fill the calendar through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and serviced-stay trade serving business parks, the University of Hertfordshire and visitors to the great house, with a guide and tour scene built around Hatfield House and the de Havilland heritage. Hatfield station on the East Coast route puts the town a short run into London King's Cross, and the A1(M) carries day-trippers in, so operators handle stopover trade as well as visitors heading across central Hertfordshire.

Bishop's Stortford.region: Bishop's Stortford and the Stort Valley
Bishop's Stortford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Stort Valley
s1loc: Bishop's Stortford runs a busy visitor economy as a historic market town on the River Stort, anchored by South Mill Arts, the former Rhodes Arts Complex, a year-round venue staging professional and local theatre, dance, live music, comedy and cinema. The town's medieval street pattern, the surviving motte of Waytemore Castle and the bustling market that has run for centuries give the centre a strong sense of place on the Hertfordshire and Essex border.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the River Stort and the Stort Navigation, where boat hire, towpath walking and cycling routes run south toward Harlow and Roydon. Grange Paddocks and the surrounding country parks, the riverside meadows and the trails through the wider Stort Valley give families and activity operators a strong outdoor offer through the warmer season, with the navigation drawing walkers and boaters across the area.

Heritage and culture run deep here. Bishop's Stortford Museum, set in two listed Victorian buildings, tells the story of Cecil Rhodes, born in the town in 1853, alongside the local history collection and the Thorley Bourne Gallery. The medieval Church of St Michael, the Corn Exchange and the Jackson Square events calendar add depth, while the historic Hockerill and Castle quarters give the town a layered character beyond the modern centre.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving business travellers, the wider district and visitors using nearby Stansted, with a guide and tour scene built around the market town and the Stort Valley. Bishop's Stortford station on the West Anglia line links the town directly to London Liverpool Street and to Stansted Airport a few minutes north, so operators handle airport and stopover trade as well as day-trippers heading into the Essex and Hertfordshire countryside.

Wokingham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Thames Valley
s1loc: Wokingham carries a steady visitor economy at the heart of the Thames Valley, anchored by Dinton Pastures Country Park, 350 acres of woodland, meadow and lakes that form an oasis in one of the most built-up parts of Berkshire. The park's lakes host sailing, kayaking and paddleboarding, while the historic Market Place, granted its charter by Henry the Third in 1219, still holds markets several days a week and anchors the regenerated town centre.

The leisure and activity layer reaches across the surrounding parkland and heath. California Country Park at Finchampstead, set within 100 acres of ancient bog and lowland heath, offers walking, a lake and a family beach area, while the Dinton Activity Centre runs outdoor pursuits for schools, families and youth groups, and the trails and green spaces around Elms Field keep activity operators busy through the warmer season across the district.

Heritage and culture centre on the restored town centre, where Elms Field, Peach Place and Carnival Place stage events, markets, fairs and festivals through the year. The Tudor and Georgian buildings around the Market Place, the historic Lucas Hospital almshouses and the events calendar running across the regenerated public spaces give Wokingham a distinct identity within the wider Thames Valley belt of towns.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and serviced-stay trade serving business parks, the Thames Valley corridor and visitors to the countryside, with a guide and day-trip scene reaching the lakes and country parks. Wokingham station links the town to Reading, London Waterloo and Guildford, and the M4 and A329(M) carry day-trippers in, so operators handle business and stopover trade as well as visitors heading for the parks and the wider Berkshire countryside.

Feltham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of west London
s1loc: Feltham sits at the heart of west London's airport belt, with Hanworth Park House, built in 1802 on the site of a Tudor palace, standing as the town's most distinctive landmark within the wide green expanse of Hanworth Park. The park was once the London Air Park, home to the National Flying Services and the scene of two Graf Zeppelin landings and Amelia Earhart's arrival in London after her solo Atlantic crossing, giving Feltham a vivid aviation heritage.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the Hanworth Air Park Leisure Centre, with its 25-metre pool, learner and toddler areas, outdoor tennis and squash courts, set behind the open green of Hanworth Park itself. The wider open spaces, the nearby Hounslow Heath nature reserve and the trails and play areas across the park give families and activity operators a busy local offer through the warmer season across the borough.

Heritage and culture draw on the town's flying past and its parkland setting, with the campaign to restore Hanworth Park House and the events programme run by Feltham Arts giving the area a cultural focus. The historic church and conservation streets of old Hanworth, the green frontage of the park and the events staged across the open space add depth to a district shaped by its aerodrome story and its place on the edge of the capital.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel and serviced-stay trade clustered around Heathrow, with Premier Inn, Travelodge and Marriott properties handling stopover, business and crew traffic just minutes from the runways. Feltham station on the South Western route links the town to London Waterloo, Twickenham and Staines, and the M3, M4 and A30 carry visitors in, so operators handle heavy airport trade alongside day-trippers heading into central London and the Thames-side towns nearby.

Farnham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of west Surrey
s1loc: Farnham runs a strong visitor economy as a historic Georgian market town on the Surrey and Hampshire border, anchored by Farnham Castle, the hilltop fortress and bishop's palace whose keep and great hall have watched over the town for nine centuries. The Museum of Farnham, set in the Georgian Willmer House on West Street, traces the town's craft and trading past, while the elegant streetscape and the ruins of Waverley Abbey nearby draw visitors across the year.

The leisure and activity layer reaches into the countryside on the town's edge. Birdworld, just outside Farnham, is home to over a thousand birds with its Penguin Beach, Owl Academy and Treetop Adventures play area, while the Rural Life Living Museum at Tilford spreads across 10 acres with its Old Kiln Light Railway running steam and diesel rides. The trails of the North Downs Way and Frensham Ponds give walkers and activity operators a busy outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Maltings arts centre on the riverside stages theatre, music, craft markets and the long-running Farnham Maltings festivals, while the Crafts Study Centre and the town's reputation as a centre for ceramics and the arts give it a distinct cultural identity. The Georgian quarter of Castle Street and West Street, the historic almshouses and the events calendar across the town fill the diary through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, inn and guest-house trade serving the market town, business travellers and visitors heading for the Surrey Hills, with a guide and tour scene built around the castle and the craft heritage. Farnham station on the line to London Waterloo and the A31 link the town to Guildford, Aldershot and the wider county, so operators handle stopover trade as well as day-trippers heading for the North Downs and the heathland country nearby.

Fareham.region: Fareham and the south Hampshire coast
Fareham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the south Hampshire coast
s1loc: Fareham runs a busy visitor economy between Portsmouth and Southampton, anchored by the Royal Armouries at Fort Nelson, a great 19th-century fortress on Portsdown Hill housing the national collection of artillery, with historic cannons, underground tunnels and panoramic views across the Solent. Portchester Castle, a remarkably preserved Roman fort later expanded into a medieval royal castle on the harbour shore, gives the area a second marquee draw steeped in centuries of coastal history.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the waterside and the wider Solent coast. Holly Hill Woodland Park offers trails, lakes and views over the River Hamble, while Titchfield Haven National Nature Reserve protects wetlands rich in wading birds, and Hill Head Beach and the Hamble draw sailors, windsurfers and walkers. The creeks, the harbour and the coastal paths give families and activity operators a strong outdoor offer through the warmer season along the shore.

Heritage and culture run deep here. Westbury Manor Museum, set in a Georgian building in the town centre, traces Fareham's maritime past and Victorian life, while the medieval ruins of Titchfield Abbey, founded in the 13th century, and the conservation streets of Old Fareham add depth. The events calendar across the town centre and the waterside, and the heritage of the harbour villages, give the area a layered character beyond the modern shopping core.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house trade serving the south Hampshire belt, business travellers and visitors to the coast, with a guide and tour scene built around Fort Nelson and Portchester Castle. Fareham station links the town along the coast to Portsmouth, Southampton and Cosham, and the M27 carries day-trippers in, so operators handle stopover trade as well as visitors heading for the Solent, the Meon Valley and the wider Hampshire coast nearby.

Chorley.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of central Lancashire
s1loc: Chorley runs a distinctive visitor economy in central Lancashire, anchored by Astley Hall, a Grade One listed Tudor and Jacobean house with roots over 400 years deep, set in its parkland and home to the town's museum and art gallery, with the neighbouring Coach House holding the Chorley Remembers Experience. The grand heritage settings of Hoghton Tower and Heskin Hall nearby give the area a strong cluster of historic houses that draw visitors across the year.

The leisure and activity layer reaches into the moors and parkland on the town's edge. Yarrow Valley Country Park spreads across more than 700 acres along the River Yarrow with woodland, lakes, trails, a visitor centre and a play area, while Rivington Country Park, Rivington Pike and the restored Terraced Gardens with their seven-arched bridge and Japanese and Italian lakes give walkers and activity operators a busy outdoor offer through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run deep here. Astley Park hosts events and shows through the year, while the historic flat-iron market in the town centre, one of the oldest open-air markets in Lancashire, and the events calendar around Astley Hall fill the diary. The grounds of the surrounding historic halls, the parkland walks and the festivals across the district give Chorley a layered character beyond its market-town centre.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving central Lancashire, business travellers and walkers heading for the West Pennine Moors, with a guide and tour scene built around the historic halls and Rivington. Chorley station links the town to Preston, Bolton and Manchester, and the M61 and M6 carry day-trippers in, so operators handle stopover trade as well as visitors heading for Rivington, the moors and the wider Lancashire countryside nearby.
